title: Claude traces NIST elliptic-curve seeds to a 1990s random-number generator
friendlyTitle: Claude explains where a common security standard came from
summary: Anthropic said on 16 October that Claude recovered how the seeds for widely used NIST elliptic curves, including P-256, were generated. They match output from the old C library function lrand48, started from Unix timestamps in 1997 and 1998, not from a secret hashed phrase. Anthropic says this is not a break or a new attack, and that it makes a deliberate backdoor less plausible.
friendlySummary: Anthropic says Claude found how the seeds for a widely used encryption standard were made. They came from an old random-number tool started with the computer's clock in 1997 and 1998, not from a hidden phrase. Anthropic says this is not a new break.
whyItMatters: These curves protect everyday signatures in browsers, phones and payment systems. Anthropic says there is nothing to change. Some published base points are still unexplained, and the researchers do not know why some other viable curves from the same runs were skipped.
friendlyWhyItMatters: These curves protect ordinary logins and payments. Anthropic says you do not need to change anything. A few related details are still unexplained.
